lesson.grammar_point: polite requests for clarification: could you / would you mind + -ing / indirect questions (could you tell me what it means?)

listenings.text: I train people for international meetings, and I always teach three simple steps. Step one: when you miss something, stop the conversation early. Say, sorry, I didn't catch that, could you rephrase it? It takes about five seconds, and nobody remembers it after the call. Step two: do not try to understand every word. Listen for the key points, the numbers, the dates and the names. Step three: at the end of the call, sum up. Say, so, to sum up, we agreed on this and this. If you misunderstood something, your partner will tell you then, and not three weeks later in the contract.

Good morning. My name is Chen, and I am an engineer at a camera company in Shenzhen. This is our new camera for hospitals. It records in color at night, even with very little light. It also counts people in a room, so the hospital knows when a waiting room is too full. At the moment, more than three hundred hospitals use this camera, in China and in other countries in Asia. Now we are looking for partners in Latin America. We can deliver to Brazil in about six weeks. If you have questions, please ask me. I know my English is fast, so please ask me to slow down.

Hi Luciana, it's Anna. I'm sorry, I'm at the airport in Munich and there is a lot of background noise here. Can you hear me? OK. I'm calling about our meeting next week. My director can't join on Tuesday, so I would like to move the meeting to Thursday, same time, ten in the morning, Sao Paulo time. Is that OK for you? And one more thing. Would you mind sending me your company profile before Thursday? My director wants to read it before the call. Sorry again for the noise. I'll send you an email with all of this when I land.

paras: Many professionals who work in a second language have the same secret: in meetings, they do not understand everything. They are not alone. Research on international teams shows that even native speakers ask for repetition several times in a one-hour call, because of accents, background noise and bad connections.

The difference between a good listener and a lost listener is not the level of English. It is what they do when they miss something. A lost listener stays quiet, smiles and hopes the point is not important. A good listener stops the conversation for five seconds: sorry, I didn’t catch that, could you rephrase it? Then she follows the rest of the meeting without stress.

Good listeners also know that they do not need every word. They listen for the gist first, and then for the key points: numbers, dates, names and decisions. At the end of the call, they sum up what they understood and double-check the numbers. Partners rarely think this is weak English. Most of them think it is a professional who does not want mistakes in the contract.
